solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sailors, American, pointing to a group of small bones

parts.note: tars is an old slang word for sailors

explanation.surface: Navy men from the States are pointed towards some tiny bones.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarsus is the cluster of small bones forming the ankle and upper foot.

clue.text: A long introduction to 'Ulysses'? So long

parts.note: to long for something is to be dying for it, so long gives die

indicators.note: an introduction is the start, so only the first letter of Ulysses is used

explanation.surface: A question whether a lengthy preface to Joyce's novel should be said goodbye to.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a preface to James Joyce's novel, but 'long' is a verb here: to long is to be dying for something.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a French farewell, like the casual English goodbye so long.

clue.text: Random inspection in locality leading to arrest

parts.note: a spot is a place or locality
to check something is to halt or arrest it

explanation.surface: Police search a neighbourhood before making an arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot check is an unannounced inspection carried out at random.

clue.text: Criminal was almost shot — does it matter?

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so a letter is dropped from shot

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A criminal was nearly shot, and someone shrugs it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the S of SHOT to leave HOT; 'Criminal' then shuffles WAS with HOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The dismissive phrase asks why anyone should care, as does the question does it matter.

clue.text: Fool, one taken in by her dressmaker?

parts.note: a clot is a British slang word for a fool

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being enclosed by it, so the numeral goes inside the word her

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A dressmaker is called a fool who has been duped by some woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothier makes or sells clothes, loosely the work of a dressmaker.

clue.text: Big old British-born actor makes one chuckle during dance

indicators.note: during means a laugh occurs in the middle of the dance, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: the Charleston is a lively 1920s dance
a single chuckle is a laugh

explanation.surface: A heavy veteran performer gets a giggle out of someone while dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one chuckle' reads as a single unit giving one word. The actor, born in Scarborough, played Henry VIII and Quasimodo before moving to Hollywood.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Laughton was a heavily built English actor of the mid twentieth century, famous in Hollywood and long dead.

clue.text: Closed small company at Inverness, for example

parts.note: something over is finished or closed
Co is the short form of company

explanation.surface: A small firm in a Scottish town has shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: Inverness looks like the Highland city, but here it is a sleeveless cape-coat named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inverness is a heavy coat with a detachable cape, one type of outer garment.

clue.text: Leave work in the course of strike

indicators.note: in the course of means within, so the short word for work goes inside the word for strike

parts.note: to strike is to hit
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone walks out from the job during industrial action.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is British slang telling someone to go away, to leave.

clue.text: Oriental Queen engaging a novelist from Ireland

indicators.note: engaging means holding within, so the queen's letters wrap around the rest

parts.note: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth
taken as written
Laurence Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy, was born in Ireland

explanation.surface: The monarch takes on an Irish-born writer of fiction from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from the East, an Oriental in dated usage, is someone from eastern lands.

clue.text: Marine mammal, captain, and law he's broken

parts.note: a pilot is in command of an aircraft, as a captain is

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of law and he are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the possessive s gives no letter; he is taken as written

explanation.surface: A sea creature, a ship's master and a law that some man has broken are listed together.
explanation.definitionFit: This species is a large toothed dolphin of the open sea, a mammal living in the ocean.

clue.text: Forgotten old man on street

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: A father living on some road has slipped from memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Something over and done with belongs to history and may be left behind in memory, as forgotten things are.

clue.text: Boozing from bar to bar, becoming crude in quiet club maybe

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, quiet

indicators.note: in places the word for crude within the shuffled club letters
maybe suggests the letters of club could be otherwise, a signal to rearrange them

parts.note: taken as written
raw means crude or unrefined

explanation.surface: Going drinking from pub to pub, someone turns uncouth in a hushed club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges the letters of club, and 'in' puts the word for crude inside them; 'becoming' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour of several pubs, drinking in each, is the British idea of a night of boozing from bar to bar.

clue.text: Clipper ship?

definitions.meaning: a person or tool that clips something is one that cuts
a small fast sailing vessel or a coastguard boat goes by this name

explanation.definitionFit: Anything that clips cuts, and the same word names a single-masted sailing boat.

clue.text: One may find me in a casino in Oxford, say

definitions.text: One may find me in a casino
definitions.meaning: a dealing box holding several decks of cards at the gaming table
an Oxford is a type of laced leather footwear

explanation.definitionFit: Casinos deal cards from a box with this name, and an Oxford is a classic laced example of footwear.

clue.text: The osprey materialised suddenly, as if by magic

indicators.note: something that materialised has taken a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird of prey appeared out of nowhere like a conjuring trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjuror's exclamation marks something appearing suddenly as though by magic.

clue.text: Understudy with good reputation

parts.note: a stand-in takes a performer's place, just as an understudy does

explanation.surface: An understudy is said to have a fine name.
explanation.definitionFit: One's position or status in others' eyes is one's reputation.

clue.text: Cashier let off

definitions.meaning: to cashier an officer is to dismiss them from the armed forces
to let off a gun or a firework is to fire it

explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers dismissing someone from service and firing a weapon or releasing something.

clue.text: Blatant publicity by band nearly takes everyone in

indicators.note: takes with in means the letters of by take in and enclose another word
in completes takes in, a phrase meaning to enclose

parts.note: taken as written
all means everyone

indicators.note: nearly means the last letter of the word for band is dropped

parts.note: a hoop is a circular band

explanation.surface: A group of musicians almost fools everyone with loud promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' drops the last letter of the word for band; 'takes ... in' wraps the first word round the word for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballyhoo is noisy, extravagant advertising or fuss, brash publicity.

clue.text: Exercises at Eastern inn before a riding event

parts.note: gym is short for gymnastics, physical exercises
a khan is a caravanserai, an inn for travellers in the Middle East and Asia

explanation.surface: Someone works out at an inn in the East before going to a horse show.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymkhana is a show of horse-riding competitions, often for children on ponies.

clue.text: Type that is dropped from operational flight

indicators.note: dropped from tells us the letters for that is are taken out of the word for the mission

parts.note: a sortie is a single mission flown by a military aircraft
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A kind of thing has been cut from a military mission.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort is a kind or type, as in 'that sort of person'.

clue.text: Bloomer over getting child in free

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for child inside the word for free

parts.note: to rid is to free

explanation.surface: A mistake over taking a child into a free place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a blunder, but here it is something that blooms, a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchid is a flowering plant, something that blooms.

clue.text: Family butcher's first to get into trouble

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so the letter goes inside the word for trouble

parts.note: a trial is an ordeal, a source of trouble

indicators.note: first selects only the opening letter of butcher's

explanation.surface: A family butcher is somehow landing in difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribal describes things belonging to a clan or kinship group, so family as an adjective, as in family loyalties.

clue.text: Child and I must go into farm building

indicators.note: must go into means one letter is placed inside the farm building

parts.note: a barn is a building on a farm

explanation.surface: A youngster and I have to get into the barn.
explanation.walkthrough: BAIRN is the Scottish and northern English word for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Bairn is the Scots word for a child.

clue.text: Swing he composed, with bit of ragtime thrown in?

definitions.text: Swing he composed, with bit of ragtime thrown in?

indicators.note: thrown in signals that the letter is added into the middle of the shuffled letters
composed suggests music arranged anew, so the letters of swing and he are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: a bit of ragtime here is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: An American composer wrote swing and added touches of ragtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' turns SWINGHE into GESHWIN, and 'thrown in' places R after GE. The whole clue also describes George Gershwin, the American composer whose work drew on jazz and ragtime.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was the American composer whose music mixed jazz, swing and ragtime styles.

clue.text: United at home, supported by everyone initially

parts.note: being in means being at home
something on another thing rests on it, supported by it

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of everyone is taken

explanation.surface: A team plays at home, backed by the whole crowd from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supported by' places the first piece above what follows; 'United' as a definition means joined together, not the football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things combined together are joined as a single unit, united.

clue.text: Up endlessly making wine

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the word for up is dropped

parts.note: astir means up and about, out of bed

explanation.surface: Someone stays up all hours making wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling white wine from Piedmont in northern Italy.

clue.text: Hot, hot fire — crackers explode!

indicators.note: crackers means crazy, so these letters go mad and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A blazing fire with fireworks going off with a bang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' looks like fireworks in the surface, but it is the anagram signal (British slang for mad).
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to lose one's temper violently, to explode with anger.

clue.text: Duke won't now broadcast in city centre

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the apostrophe gives no letter; the word is taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A duke refuses to go on air now in the heart of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Downtown is the American word for the central business district of a city.

clue.text: Buys it on the Spanish train

parts.note: to buy it is slang for to die, so buys it means dies
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone gets killed aboard a train in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A train hauled by a locomotive running on diesel fuel is often simply called by that name.
